The Salford children's home run by Cambian Childcare Ltd went from an "outstanding" rating to "inadequate" in all areas, with Ofsted inspectors finding "the experiences of children and young people are poor and they are not making progress". Cambian Childcare Ltd said since the inspection it has resolved issues raised in the report. That led to further "distress and instability" for the child, according to the inspector. The recently published report pointed to staffing as a potential cause of the problems. Inspector Michelle Snape said: "Children who have lived in the home have not been cared for by a consistent staff team. "Five staff have left since the last inspection and staff from the manager's other home have been supporting the children. This does not help children to build meaningful and trusted relationships." "Though positive, this is far below the 55% reduction targeted for that period to stay within the city's carbon budget." title: Bolton's walking and cycling route upgrades to begin

input.lead: Phase one of the £5m project will focus on Bradshawgate and Great Moor Street
input.summary: Phase one of the £5m project will focus on Bradshawgate and Great Moor Street
input.evidence_text: Bolton's walking and cycling route upgrades to begin - BBC News Image source, Bolton Council Image caption, Phase one of the project will focus on Bradshawgate and Great Moor Street By Chris Gee Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 1 hour ago A £5m project to improve walking and cycling routes in Bolton is to begin next week. The work will be carried out in the town centre from Monday, with phase one of the scheme focusing on resurfacing roads and repaving footpaths on Bradshawgate and Great Moor Street. There will also be changes at side roads to give pedestrians priority, along with an upgraded pedestrian crossing on Bradshawgate, near Nelson Square. Bolton Council said its plan to "transform the town centre" would make it an area people could all "enjoy and be proud of". As well as the repaving and resurfacing, four junctions will be upgraded to make it easier and safer for people on foot and riding bikes to travel around the town centre. Throughout construction, the council said traffic management will be in place with "disruption kept to a minimum". Funding was first granted in 2023 from the Greater Manchester Mayor's Cycling and Walking Challenge Fund and the council carried out consultation that helped shape the plans, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. But work was delayed by the need to prepare for the demolition and regeneration of Crompton Place. With the removal of Crompton Place now underway, the council said work on the travel improvements can begin. Coun Nadeem Ayub, Bolton Council's executive member for highways, transport and planning, said: "As we progress our ambitious plans to transform the town centre, it is vital that we include better ways for people to move around. input.summary: Zak Bolland was released 13 days before he murdered a woman and four children in a firebomb attack
input.evidence_text: Salford firebomb killer released by police despite 'last chance' warning - BBC News Image source, Family photos Image caption, The four Pearson children died during the petrol bomb attack, and their mother died 20 months later Published 6 October 2026 A man who murdered a mother and her four children in a firebomb attack had been arrested and released by police a fortnight before, despite a judge having told him he was on his "last chance", an inquest has heard. Zak Bolland, then 23, left a police station after giving a 12-minute "no comment" interview for breaking windows at the home of Michelle Pearson, 37, and her young family in Walkden, Salford, Greater Manchester, on 26 November 2017. Bolland's record was not checked at the time and he was told no further action would be taken, Bolton Coroner's Court heard. Thirteen days later he petrol bombed the house, killing the children and severely burning their mother, who died 20 months later. Demi, 15, her brother Brandon, eight, and seven-year-old sister Lacie, who were sleeping in a front bedroom, all died in the blaze. Michelle suffered 68% burns to her body and "clung on to life" until she died on 25 August 2019. On the second day of an eight-week inquest, police who had been involved with the family before the fatal attack were questioned. PC John Worthington of Greater Manchester Police (GMP) told the inquest he went to the house after the windows were smashed and Bolland was named as the culprit. The council said the decisions it was making, and "even the ones we haven't made yet" were all "regrettable". 'Won't be enough' Trafford Council is the other, and two years into receiving EFS, residents have seen council tax increases of 7.49% each year. Finance leaders at Bury have stated they do not believe borrowing was the solution for the council, but did not rule out tax rises of more than 4.99% if the government allowed it. title: Sue Cleaver hails Victoria Wood legacy as she joins Dinnerladies stage tour

input.lead: The stage adaptation of Victoria Wood's beloved sitcom will have a run at the Manchester Opera House
input.summary: The stage adaptation of Victoria Wood's beloved sitcom will have a run at the Manchester Opera House
input.evidence_text: Sue Cleaver hails Victoria Wood legacy as she joins Dinnerladies stage tour - BBC News Image caption, Victoria Wood wrote and played Brenda, the deputy canteen manager, in the BBC TV comedy show Dinnerladies Published 6 October 2026 Actress Sue Cleaver has said Victoria Wood would be "over the moon" with a new stage adaptation of beloved sitcom Dinnerladies, which she hailed as "a celebration of her legacy". Best known as Eileen Grimshaw in ITV soap Coronation Street, Cleaver is among the famous faces joining the new production, which is the first to be commissioned by Wood's estate since her death in 2016 at the age of 62. The 63-year-old, who featured in the BBC show as a recurring character, will take the stage as cynical canteen worker Jean, who was played by Anne Reid in the show. She said the script it "blew her away" and that it had been "beautifully adapted" from Wood's show. The show, created, written and co-produced by Wood, aired on the BBC from 1998 to 2000 and followed the workplace dramas of the staff and regulars in a canteen at a factory in Manchester. More than 25 years on, Cleaver told BBC Radio Manchester the sitcom, which ran for two series was "observational comedy at its finest". She said: "I'm thrilled to be doing it. "It's such a celebration of Vic's work. It's about the celebration of her and her legacy. "I think she'd be over the moon and I'm very excited to be a part of it." Cleaver added: "There's no way [the audience] are not going to be able to enjoy this show. "It's a British classic and nobody writes the way Vic writes. "If you've never been in a theatre in your life, make this the one time that you do come because it won't let you down." If nothing changes, leaders predict their three-budget gap could hit £35m Even with identified savings, that gap would still be £9.6m for the coming financial year 2027/28, rising to £17.5m at the end of three years. Town halls are legally bound to present a balanced budget each year or must file a Section 114 notice, effectively declaring themselves b This announcement makes Bury council the second Greater Manchester authority to apply for EFS in recent years, with Trafford council currently in its second year of emergency aid . For Trafford residents, this has resulted in two years of huge council tax rises with increases at Finance leads at Bury council sat down with the Manchester Evening News to set out the authority’s position. I caught the 590 this week as far as Hebden Bridge as part of our occasional series on Greater Manchester's most scenic bus routes The first thing to note is because this is a privately-owned First Bus and not a publicly-controlled Bee Network service a single ticket is £2.50 not two quid. input.summary: Oldham Council has approved a new package of interim governance arrangements
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has approved a new package of interim governance arrangements. These measures are designed to strengthen democratic oversight, provide clear political leadership across key service areas and support transparent decision-making while the borough continues to work towards the appointment of a Council Leader and Cabinet. The arrangements were approved by Council on 16 September and include the creation of interim Lead Member and Deputy Lead Member roles aligned to the Council's four directorates. The arrangements form part of a wider governance framework developed following legal advice, engagement with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, and discussions between political group leaders. Under the arrangements, Chief Executive Shelley Kipling will continue to exercise delegated executive powers, while Lead Members provide political oversight, advocacy and a visible link between residents, councillors and services. The roles carry no executive decision-making powers. The four Interim Lead Member portfolios have been allocated to the Council's four largest political groups, with deputy roles assigned from the same groups. Interim Lead Member appointments Resources - Lead Member: Sam Al-Hamdani (Liberal Democrats) - Deputy Lead Member: Mark Kenyon (Liberal Democrats) The Resources portfolio will provide political oversight of the Council's finances, budget management, transformation programme, corporate services, governance, workforce and organisational performance. title: Council secures court order following unauthorised encampment at Oldham Edge

input.lead: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.summary: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge. Council officers first visited the site on Thursday 6th August following concerns from residents and people using the park. Officers spoke to those at the encampment, who said they intended to leave by Saturday 8th August. As the site had not been vacated, the Council returned with support from Greater Manchester Police on Tuesday 11th August. A formal direction was served under Section 77 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, requiring those at the encampment to leave and remove their vehicles and belongings. The Council also provided information about authorised sites in Greater Manchester, along with advice about health, wellbeing and reporting hate crime. After the direction was not followed, the Council began court proceedings. On Monday 17th August, Tameside Magistrates’ Court granted an order requiring the removal of the encampment. The site was vacated later that day. A significant amount of waste was left behind, which has now been removed by the Council’s cleansing team. A Council spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents and people using Oldham Edge, and we thank them for their patience while we followed the legal process. “We always try to resolve unauthorised encampments through discussion and voluntary cooperation wherever possible. However, when the site was not vacated as agreed, it became necessary to take further action. “We worked closely with Greater Manchester Police throughout to make sure the situation was handled lawfully and proportionately. “The encampment has now left and our cleansing team has completed the clean-up, allowing the area to be returned to the local community.”

title: Beat the Jams Autumn season announced

input.lead: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians.
input.summary: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians. Beat the Jams live […] The post Beat the Jams Autumn season announced appeared first on Band on the Wall
input.evidence_text: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians. Beat the Jams live series showcases the very best of the jazz scene, at short rush hour gigs from 6pm at Band on the Wall. What better way to avoid those endless queues, chaotic traffic and stressful homeward journeys? Clock off and skip the rush-hour traffic while you watch live jazz and make the most of our happy hour deals from 5–7pm: £4.50 pints / 2 for £15 cocktails / £15 bottles of wine + pizzas from £5! The new season kicks off on 24 September with tenor saxophonist Dean Masser and pianist Richard Wetherall, followed by: 7 October – Anna Chandler-King Quartet Leeds based saxophonist and composer Anna joins us again for Beat the Jams, this time with her own band. Anna’s thoughtful and inventive compositions are firm favourites of us at Beat the Jams and her quartet promises to be a unique rush hour busting treat! 16 November – Sam Lightwing Quartet Saxophonist and composer Sam Lightwing brings presents brand new music for his thrilling young quartet, showcasing Sam’s original compositions, which blend classic mainstream jazz grooves with modern flavours of post-pop and latin, all wrapped up in the language of contemporary sax giants such as Chris Potter, Seamus Blake and Joshua Redman. 15 December – Svarc/Devine/Walsh with Richard Iles The band combines deep pocket, fearless interplay and a shared love of exploration. Expect everything from soulful melodies and infectious rhythms to moments of exhilarating collective improvisation, delivered with the chemistry that only world-class musicians can create. Tickets from £13 per show, or £42 for a season ticket

input.evidence_text: We’re inviting young people to explore music for film and compose their own soundtrack this summer! Whether your child already attends our Saturday Music Club, or just wants to try something new, our Young Musician’s Summer School is suitable for all abilities! The course will conclude with a live performance soundtracking the film for family and friends. We welcome all abilities and instruments to take part in this course. You can bring your own instruments, but we have keyboards, guitars, bass, violins, drums and percussion on site which can be used if you don’t have an instrument. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round
